about: English idiom -> the HINDI IDIOM used in the same situation. Never the literal words, and never a plain-language paraphrase: a paraphrase is accurate but reads like a textbook, and the point of this file is that a listener should hear what a Hindi speaker would actually say.
PROVENANCE — READ THIS BEFORE TRUSTING T: The Hindi in this file was written from the author's own knowledge. It was NOT taken from a Hindi idiom dictionary, a parallel corpus, a HuggingFace dataset, Reddit usage, or any published collection of muhavare, and it has NOT been checked by a native speaker.

verify.py does NOT close this gap. It proves the MECHANICS — that the placeholder survives, that the splice lands, that the surrounding Hindi agrees, that the entry doesn't fire on a literal use. It cannot tell you whether the chosen Hindi is the RIGHT idiom, or a real idiom, or one anybody actually says.

Not every entry meets the brief. Some are genuine, well-attested idioms (चेहरे का रंग उड़ जाना, घिसी-पिटी बात, फिसड्डी). Others are only better plain translations — 'सर्वोच्च शिखर' for high-water mark is a plain compound, not an idiom, and it was chosen over the more idiomatic पराकाष्ठा purely because पराकाष्ठा is feminine and broke the surrounding agreement. That is a real trade of idiomaticity for mechanical safety, and it should be revisited, not hidden.
Each entry carries a `confidence` field saying which of the two it is. Treat anything not marked well-attested as a candidate for replacement once a proper source or a native speaker is consulted.
how_to_add_an_entry: 1. 'en' lists English surface forms that all mean the same thing. Whitespace and straight-vs-curly apostrophes are handled for you; case is ignored. Word order and tense are NOT guessed, so spell out the variants you want to catch.
2. 'hi' is the replacement. It is dropped verbatim into the slot the placeholder left, so it must read correctly in that position.

3. 'span' is the real decision. The translator inflects the words AROUND the placeholder and, having no noun to agree with, assumes masculine-singular. So: use span 'clause' (mask a whole clause) whenever the Hindi is a predicate or is feminine, and reserve span 'phrase' for short reusable entries whose Hindi is masculine or invariant.

4. 'sample' MUST be the real full sentence the idiom appeared in, never a trimmed version of it. The translator builds a different frame around the placeholder depending on the rest of the sentence, so a short sample can pass while the real line breaks. This is not hypothetical: a bare 'on parade' entry verified clean against a trimmed sample and then produced 'नुमाइश पर की' in the actual talk.
5. Run `python verify.py` after adding anything. It puts every entry through the real translator and flags a splice that came out wrong. Do not trust an entry you have not verified.
6. Adding an entry needs no code change. This file is data.

en: you can see the blood run from their face
you can see the blood drain from their face
you could see the blood run from their face
entries.hi: आप देख सकते हैं कि उनके चेहरे का रंग उड़ जाता है
entries.sense: they go pale with dread at the news
entries.sample: You say you work in education, you can see the blood run from their face.

en: who gets all the brownie points
entries.sense: who collects all the credit and approval
entries.sample: Who gets all the brownie points, who are the winners.

entries.sense: the peak, the highest point ever reached. Deliberately masculine: the feminine पराकाष्ठा makes the translator emit 'के पराकाष्ठा' instead of 'की'.
entries.confidence: plain-translation, not a Hindi idiom — see the provenance note at the top of this file
counter_examples: You can see the high-water mark on the wall from the flood.
The high-water mark of the river was three metres up the bank.
entries.sample: We shouldn't hold them up as the high-water mark of all human achievement.

entries.sense: a joke or story told so often it has gone stale
counter_examples: We sat under the old chestnut tree in the garden.
The old chestnut roasting on the fire smelled wonderful.

entries.sense: stop bothering me, let me be
counter_examples: Give me a break of ten minutes between the sessions.
entries.sample: Terry, please, I'm trying to fry an egg in here. Give me a break.

entries.sense: out of time with the music. The literal reading turns 'beat' into a heartbeat.
entries.confidence: correct and natural, though a plain phrase rather than a fixed idiom
counter_examples: The constable walked off the beat and went home.
She stepped off the beat and onto the pavement.
entries.sample: Grown men and women writhing uncontrollably, off the beat.

entries.hi: वो अपने ही ख़यालों में जीते हैं
entries.sense: they are lost in thought, disconnected from their bodies. The literal version also flips the pronoun, making them live inside SOMEONE ELSE's head.
entries.sample: Not all of them, but typically, they live in their heads.

entries.hi: वो पढ़ाई में बिल्कुल फिसड्डी थी
entries.sense: she was very bad at schoolwork. The literal Hindi says she FELT hopeless, which is the wrong sense entirely.
entries.confidence: फिसड्डी is well-attested for exactly this (bad at studies). NOTE the Hindi hard-codes 'पढ़ाई' (schoolwork), so the guards below keep it to school contexts.
counter_examples: The nurse said she was really hopeless about her recovery chances.
entries.sample: When she was at school, she was really hopeless.

entries.hi: हम उसे खोते चले जाते हैं
entries.sense: we lose it as we get older. The literal Hindi ('we grow outside of it') is nonsense.
entries.sample: We don't grow into creativity, we grow out of it.

en: all the expertise that's been on parade for the past four days
entries.hi: पिछले चार दिनों से सामने रखी गई तमाम विशेषज्ञता
entries.sense: all the expertise that has been on display. Narrow on purpose: a bare 'on parade' entry was tried and REMOVED. Google treats the placeholder as a noun modifier here and emits 'X की विशेषज्ञता', so every short splice produced the broken 'नुमाइश पर की'. A literal parade is also a real sense of the phrase, so the short form was wrong more often than right. A narrow entry that is correct beats a broad one that is not.
entries.sample: Nobody has a clue, despite all the expertise that's been on parade for the past four days, what the world will look like in five years' time.

entries.hi: वो कोशिश कर ही डालते हैं
entries.sense: they will give it a try anyway. The literal Hindi turns a willing attempt into an obligation ('they will HAVE TO try').
entries.sample: If they don't know, they'll have a go.

entries.hi: बच्चे रिस्क ले ही लेते हैं
entries.sense: kids are willing to risk being wrong. The literal Hindi reads as taking an opportunity, which loses the risk.
entries.sample: What these things have in common is that kids will take a chance.

en: they pin you to the wall
entries.hi: वो आपको सवालों से घेर लेते हैं
entries.sense: they corner you and press you hard about it
entries.confidence: natural Hindi; सवालों से घेरना is idiomatic for being pressed with questions
counter_examples: They pin you to the wall with those clips when they measure your height.
entries.sample: But if you ask about their education, they pin you to the wall.
